1. Core Clinical Tension: A 30-year-old female farmer from Nepal presents with a 3-year history of recurrent hemoptysis, chest pain, and cough, accelerating over the preceding month. Chest CT demonstrates a well-defined cystic mass with internal air foci and bronchial communication in the right lower lobe. The indolent hemoptoic presentation and cavitary/cystic imaging simulate pulmonary tuberculosis, bacterial lung abscess, or congenital bronchogenic cyst, while the pathognomonic history of expectorating whitish membranes with a bitter taste (hydatidoptysis) reveals an underlying ruptured hydatid cyst secondarily colonized by saprophytic fungi.
2. Admission Breakpoint: The breakpoint occurs after the clinical history, physical examination (decreased breath sounds at the right lung base), normal baseline labs (absence of peripheral eosinophilia, normal leukocytes, negative sputum acid-fast smears), abdominal ultrasound excluding hepatic lesions, and chest CT revealing the right lower lobe cystic lesion with bronchial communication, immediately prior to thoracotomy, operative exploration, and histopathological analysis.
3. Differential Distinctions: Pulmonary tuberculosis presents with chronic hemoptysis and cavitary lesions in high-burden settings but is excluded by lack of B-symptoms and negative sputum AFB stains. Bacterial lung abscess presents with fever, purulent sputum, marked leukocytosis, and thick irregular wall enhancement. Bronchogenic cysts are congenital mediastinal or parenchymal cysts that rarely manifest with expectoration of grape-skin-like membrane fragments. The presence of laminated cuticular membranes confirms Echinococcus, which predisposes to fungal superinfection when ruptured into the airway.
case_prompt:
A 30-year-old female farmer and lifelong non-smoker presented with a three-year history of intermittent hemoptysis, which had markedly increased in frequency and volume over the preceding 30 days, accompanied by persistent cough and right-sided chest pain.

Her illness began three years earlier with episodes of coughing up blood once or twice monthly. Seven months after symptom onset, she was treated empirically at an outside clinic for pneumonia, but episodic hemoptysis persisted. Approximately one year prior to presentation, she experienced two discrete episodes during which she expectorated whitish membranous fragments mixed with blood, accompanied by a distinct sour and bitter taste in her mouth. She reported no fever, night sweats, dyspnea, anorexia, or weight loss. She had no history of chronic pulmonary illness or known chronic pulmonary contacts. She resided in a rural jungle-adjacent community in Nepal and reported continuous, prolonged contact with domesticated dogs.

On physical examination, she was comfortable and hemodynamically stable. Blood pressure was 118/70 mmHg, pulse rate 80 beats per minute, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 97% on ambient air, and body temperature 98.0°F (36.7°C). Chest examination revealed decreased vesicular breath sounds over the right hemithorax without wheezes or crackles. The remainder of the physical examination was unremarkable.

Laboratory evaluation revealed a hemoglobin level of 12.0 g/dL, normal total and differential white blood cell counts, and an absence of peripheral eosinophilia. Serum chemistries, liver function tests, and renal panels were normal. Serial sputum smears were negative for special-stain micro-organisms. Serologic screening was nonreactive for hepatitis B surface antigen and HIV antibodies. Abdominal ultrasonography demonstrated a normal liver without focal cystic or solid lesions. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography of the chest revealed a well-defined, non-enhancing cystic lesion measuring in the anterior basal segment of the right lower lobe abutting the major fissure, containing multiple internal air foci and demonstrating communication with a segmental bronchus, with associated segmental atelectasis and elevation of the right hemidiaphragm.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Considered the leading initial diagnosis given the high endemicity in Nepal, three-year history of episodic hemoptysis, productive cough, and a cavitary/cystic pulmonary lesion with internal air foci. Ruled out by the absence of constitutional symptoms (fever, night sweats, weight loss), absence of contacts, and serial negative sputum smears for acid-fast bacilli.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: She denied a history of fever, shortness of breath, night sweats, significant weight loss, contact with TB... Sputum smears were negative for acid-fast bacilli.

diagnostic_reasoning.candidate: Bacterial Lung Abscess / Chronic Necrotizing Pneumonia
diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Considered because the patient had previously received empiric antibiotic treatment for pneumonia and presented with persistent cough, hemoptysis, and an air-containing cavitary lesion communicating with a bronchus. Ruled out by the normal total leukocyte count, absence of fever or purulence, and chest CT findings of a sharply demarcated, thin-walled, non-enhancing cystic lesion rather than an irregularly enhancing inflammatory abscess.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: Total and differential leukocyte counts were within normal limits... Her chest CT upon presentation showed well-defined nonenhancing cystic lesion in the anterior basal segment of the right lower lobe adjacent to a major fissure.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Considered due to the well-defined cystic appearance adjacent to the airways with internal air and hemoptysis. Ruled out by the lack of soft tissue contrast enhancement, young non-smoking profile, and the history of coughing up whitish membranous pieces (hydatidoptysis).
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: Around a year back from now, she noticed the presence of whitish pieces mixed with blood for 2 episodes while coughing up, which was associated with a sour/bitter taste in her mouth.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: The diagnostic pivot occurred upon histopathological examination of the surgically resected pulmonary cyst, which demonstrated the pathognomonic acellular laminated membrane of an echinococcal ectocyst, with secondary intra-cavitary colonization by Aspergillus featuring dichotomously branching septate hyphae.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: What was exceptional was the presence of a laminated membrane of the ectocyst along with fungal elements (Aspergillus) in the form of septate hyphae with acute angle branching in hematoxylin and eosin stain (H&E)... This led us to the final diagnosis of coinfection by Echinococcus and Aspergillus.

editor_comments: Admission breakpoint placed following CT chest and baseline lab workup prior to thoracotomy and histopathology. Zero disease/pathogen spoilers in case_prompt. Direct verbatim quotes from case text verify differential rule-outs and diagnostic pivot. Target canonical disease Echinococcosis verified.
